vignette:
Priya is thirty-seven, married for eleven years, and the owner of a small fabric and sari shop in a strip mall on the edge of the city. She opens the shop six days a week at nine in the morning, and she stays until seven at night. She does this because if she stays home, she cannot stop thinking.

The assault happened two years ago, in the stockroom of her own shop. A man she had seen a few times before-a delivery driver for a wholesaler-came in during the afternoon lull. She knew him. He was friendly, always smiling. That day he asked to use the restroom, and she said yes. When he came out, she was alone at the counter, restocking bangles. He walked past her, and then he did not keep walking.

She does not remember all of it. The memory comes in flashes, like photographs that hurt to look at. His hand over her mouth. The tile floor cold on her back. A shelf of folded dupattas falling on them both. She remembers thinking, don't make noise, the shop next door will hear, which makes no sense now. She remembers the bell on the door chiming-a customer-and the man pulling up his jeans and walking out like nothing. The customer, an older woman, asked if Priya had any green silk. Priya stood up, straightened her kameez, and showed her the green silk.

She did not tell anyone for six months. Not her husband, not her mother, not her sister. She told herself it was not that bad. She told herself she had not said no clearly enough. She told herself she was overreacting. But her body did not believe her. She stopped being able to be touched. When her husband reached for her in bed, her whole body would lock. She would lie perfectly still, breathing slowly, waiting for him to stop trying. He thought she was angry at him. She let him think that. It was easier.

At the shop, she began to change. She took the delivery driver's number off the vendor list. She stopped ordering from that wholesaler. She started keeping the stockroom door locked. She checked it three times before she sat down behind the counter. And she started to watch the door. Every time the bell chimed, a spike of heat went through her chest. If a man walked in alone, her hands would start to shake. She would force herself to smile, but her voice came out too high. She learned to keep the counter between herself and any male customer. She learned to read their eyes, their hands, the way they stood. Every man became a potential threat. She could not stop scanning, assessing, bracing.

The memories started coming at night. She would wake up at three in the morning with her heart pounding, convinced she heard footsteps in the hallway. Once, she screamed-a short, choked sound-and her husband sat up, terrified, asking what was wrong. She said she had a nightmare. She did not tell him what kind.

She started washing her hands constantly. The feeling of the stockroom floor on her skin stayed with her, like a residue. She would scrub her palms until they were raw. She stopped wearing the salwar she had worn that day, even though it was her favorite, blue with gold embroidery. She threw it away. She could not stand to look at it.

At work, she became hypervigilant. She kept her phone in her apron pocket at all times. She memorized the layout of the shop-where the back exit was, which shelf could hide her if she needed to crouch. She started locking the front door during slow hours, even though it hurt business. She would tell customers she was restocking. She did not want to explain.

The worst part is the guilt. She replays it endlessly. Why did I let him use the restroom? Why didn't I scream? Why didn't I tell my husband? She blames herself for being too nice, too trusting. She blames herself for staying silent. She feels dirty and wrong and alone. She has not touched her husband in almost two years. She has not let anyone touch her. She has stopped going to family gatherings because she cannot stand to be in a room full of people, smiling, pretending she is fine.

She is not fine. She is exhausted. She is afraid of the bell on her own shop door. She is afraid of the night. She is afraid of her own mind. But every morning she showers, braids her hair, puts on her work clothes, and unlocks the shop. She does not know what else to do.
